title: Cumulative Distribution Function
subtitle: Defining F_X(x) = P(X ≤ x), its properties, and how to read it as a step function for discrete random variables

concepts.title: Bernoulli example: CDF as a step function
Recovering PMF from CDF: jumps = probabilities
General discrete CDF: same staircase structure

annotations.title: Notation: F_X(x) vs F(x)
annotations.body: F_X(x) is the CDF of the random variable X, evaluated at the real number x. The subscript X identifies which random variable's CDF we mean (useful when several are floating around); the argument x is the point at which we evaluate it. Many books drop the subscript when context is clear and write F(x). Both are standard.

annotations.title: Concept check: the interval formula
annotations.question: Suppose F_X(5) = 0.7 and F_X(2) = 0.3 for some random variable X. What is P(2 < X ≤ 5)?
options: 0.7, taking the CDF value at the upper endpoint
0.4, taking the difference F_X(5) − F_X(2) of the two CDF values
0.3, taking the CDF value at the lower endpoint
1.0, taking the sum F_X(5) + F_X(2) which exceeds 1 (clipped)
annotations.hint: Apply the formula P(a < X ≤ b) = F_X(b) − F_X(a) with a = 2 and b = 5.
annotations.explanation: P(2 < X ≤ 5) = F_X(5) − F_X(2) = 0.7 − 0.3 = 0.4. Two things to internalize: differences of CDF values give interval probabilities, and the left endpoint is excluded (strict inequality) while the right is included.

distractorRationale.0: Forgot to subtract the lower CDF value; took just F_X(5)
distractorRationale.2: Read off the wrong endpoint, F_X(2), as if the lower value were the answer
distractorRationale.3: Added instead of subtracted (then awkwardly clipped to 1) — sign error revealing impossible probabilities

annotations.title: Why the filled/open circles matter
annotations.body: The filled circle at the top of a jump and the open circle at the bottom encode an important convention: the CDF takes the upper value at the jump point. Formally, this is called right-continuity. It's a direct consequence of the definition F_X(x) = P(X ≤ x) — note the ≤, not <. At x = 0 for a Bernoulli RV, the event X ≤ 0 includes X = 0, so F_X(0) includes the probability mass at 0.

annotations.title: Concept check: reading PMF from CDF
annotations.question: A discrete random variable X has CDF that jumps by 0.2 at x = 3, by 0.5 at x = 7, and by 0.3 at x = 10. What is P(X = 7)?
options: 0.2, the size of the jump at x = 3 (the lowest value in the support)
0.5, the size of the jump at x = 7 (the value asked about)
0.7, the cumulative height of the CDF just after x = 7
0.3, the size of the jump at x = 10 (the highest value in the support)
annotations.hint: Each jump's height equals the probability of the variable taking that value.
annotations.explanation: P(X = 7) = 0.5, the size of the jump at x = 7. The PMF is recovered from a discrete CDF by reading off jump heights: where the CDF jumps by p at value x, the random variable takes that value with probability p. Flat regions correspond to P(X = x) = 0.

distractorRationale.0: Read the wrong jump — picked the first one (at x = 3) without matching to the asked value
distractorRationale.2: Reported the CDF height after the jump (0.2 + 0.5 = 0.7) instead of the jump size itself
distractorRationale.3: Read the wrong jump — picked the last one (at x = 10) without matching to the asked value

annotations.title: Setup for what's coming next
annotations.body: The uniform-on-{1, ..., 100} example coming up is staged to make a key point: for the discrete uniform, F_X(3.2) and F_X(3) give the same value (3/100), because the CDF is flat between integer jumps. In lecture 4.3 we'll compare this to a continuous approximation where F(x) = x/100 — and you'll see the small but useful difference between the exact discrete CDF and its continuous approximation.

annotations.title: What you should take away
annotations.body: Three things. (1) The CDF is F_X(x) = P(X ≤ x), a function from ℝ to [0, 1]. (2) It is non-decreasing, starts at 0 at −∞, ends at 1 at +∞, and for discrete RVs it's a staircase with jumps at the values the RV can take. (3) Interval probabilities come from differences: P(a < X ≤ b) = F_X(b) − F_X(a). These three facts are the entire toolkit you need for the next lecture, where the CDF becomes the bridge to continuous random variables.

questions.question: What is the correct definition of the cumulative distribution function F_X(x)?
options: F_X(x) = P(X = x), the probability of taking exactly the value x
F_X(x) = P(X ≤ x), the probability of taking any value up to and including x
F_X(x) = P(X < x), the probability of taking any value strictly below x
F_X(x) = P(X ≥ x), the probability of taking any value at or above x
questions.hint: Watch the inequality carefully. The 'cumulative' in CDF refers to accumulating probability from the left, and includes the endpoint.
questions.explanation: F_X(x) = P(X ≤ x). The ≤ is essential: it includes the value x itself, which is what produces right-continuity (the filled circle at jumps). P(X = x) is the PMF; P(X < x) gives the left-continuous version; P(X ≥ x) is the survival function. The standard CDF uses ≤.

distractorRationale.0: Conflates PMF with CDF — a foundational confusion this lecture is explicitly addressing
distractorRationale.2: Off-by-one inequality error: strict less-than instead of less-than-or-equal; produces left-continuity instead of right-continuity
distractorRationale.3: Confuses CDF with survival function S(x) = 1 − F_X(x), a related but distinct object

questions.question: A random variable X has F_X(4) = 0.6 and F_X(9) = 0.85. What is P(4 < X ≤ 9)?
options: 0.85 − 0 = 0.85 (the value at the upper endpoint)
0.85 − 0.6 = 0.25 (difference of CDF values at the endpoints)
0.85 + 0.6 = 1.45 (sum of CDF values at the endpoints)
(0.85 + 0.6) / 2 = 0.725 (midpoint of the two CDF values)
questions.hint: Apply the interval formula P(a < X ≤ b) = F_X(b) − F_X(a) directly with a = 4 and b = 9.
questions.explanation: P(4 < X ≤ 9) = F_X(9) − F_X(4) = 0.85 − 0.6 = 0.25. The difference of CDF values gives the probability of the interval. Differences are the workhorse computation with CDFs.

distractorRationale.0: Forgot to subtract the lower endpoint; treated F_X(9) alone as the answer
distractorRationale.2: Sign error — added instead of subtracted; produces values that can exceed 1, which should immediately flag the mistake
distractorRationale.3: Misapplied a 'midpoint' or 'average' intuition; CDFs don't combine that way

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a required property of every cumulative distribution function?
options: F_X(x) is non-decreasing in x throughout the entire real line
F_X(x) is differentiable at every point in its domain, including jumps
F_X(x) tends to 0 at minus infinity and tends to 1 at plus infinity
F_X(x) takes values in the closed interval [0, 1] for every x
questions.hint: Think about the CDF of a discrete random variable — does it have jumps? Can a function with jumps be differentiable at those points?
questions.explanation: A CDF must be non-decreasing, bounded in [0, 1], and have limits 0 at −∞ and 1 at +∞. But it need not be differentiable: discrete CDFs have jumps, where the derivative doesn't exist. Differentiability is a feature of continuous CDFs specifically, not a universal requirement.

distractorRationale.0: Genuinely required, not the exception — but a student who confused 'non-decreasing' with 'strictly increasing' might wrongly think this is the loose property
distractorRationale.2: Genuinely required and unambiguous; a student picking this might be guessing the question is a trick about boundary behavior
distractorRationale.3: Genuinely required; a student picking this is confusing 'takes values in [0,1]' (probability axiom) with 'must equal 0 or 1' (which is false)

questions.question: For a Bernoulli random variable X with P(X = 1) = 0.3, what is F_X(0)?
options: 0, because no values below 0 are possible for a Bernoulli random variable
0.3, because that is the probability of the other value the variable takes
1, because the CDF saturates immediately for a discrete random variable
questions.hint: F_X(0) = P(X ≤ 0). Which Bernoulli values satisfy X ≤ 0? Compute P of those.
questions.explanation: F_X(0) = P(X ≤ 0). For a Bernoulli RV taking 0 or 1, X ≤ 0 means X = 0, and P(X = 0) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7. The ≤ in the CDF definition is the key: at x = 0, the CDF value includes the probability mass at 0 (right-continuity, represented as a filled circle in the sketch).
questions.concept: Bernoulli example: CDF as a step function

distractorRationale.0: Inequality error: treats F_X(0) as if the inequality were strict (< 0), missing the right-continuity convention
distractorRationale.2: Reads off P(X = 1) by mistake — perhaps confused the question about Bernoulli's two values
distractorRationale.3: Confuses 'discrete CDF' with 'instantly saturating'; only true for x ≥ the largest value (1, not 0)

questions.question: You are shown the CDF of an unknown discrete random variable. It has jumps of size 0.4 at x = 2, size 0.35 at x = 5, and size 0.25 at x = 8. Which of the following best describes the PMF?
questions.hint: Each jump in a discrete CDF corresponds to a probability mass at that value; the jump's height equals P(X = that value).
questions.explanation: The PMF is recovered from the CDF by reading off jump heights: where the CDF jumps by p at value x, the random variable takes value x with probability p. So P(X = 2) = 0.4, P(X = 5) = 0.35, P(X = 8) = 0.25, and these sum to 1 as required.
questions.concept: Recovering PMF from CDF: jumps = probabilities

distractorRationale.0: PMF/CDF confusion: reads the jump heights as CDF values, not as jump-step probabilities
distractorRationale.2: Cumulative confusion: adds jumps progressively, reporting the CDF height at each step instead of the individual jump size
distractorRationale.3: Reversed assignment: maps jump sizes to values in reverse order (0.25 to x=2 instead of x=8)

questions.question: Let X be uniform on {1, 2, …, 100}. Using the CDF, what is P(X > 87)?
options: F_X(87) = 87/100, since 87 is the threshold being asked about
1 − F_X(87) = 13/100, using the complement of the CDF at 87
1/100, since exactly one integer value sits at the boundary
F_X(87) − F_X(0) = 87/100, taking the difference from zero
questions.hint: P(X > 87) is the complement of P(X ≤ 87). Use F_X(87) and subtract from 1.
questions.explanation: P(X > 87) = 1 − P(X ≤ 87) = 1 − F_X(87) = 1 − 87/100 = 13/100. There are 13 values (88, 89, …, 100), each with probability 1/100, totaling 13/100. The complement rule via the CDF is the cleanest way.

distractorRationale.0: Forgot to take the complement — reports F_X(87) directly when the question asks about the right tail
distractorRationale.2: Confuses 'P(X > 87)' with 'P(X = 88)' or 'the probability of the next single value', getting 1/100
distractorRationale.3: Correct arithmetic but wrong setup; subtracts from F_X(0) = 0 instead of taking the complement

questions.question: Consider integer-valued X with the formula P(a < X ≤ b) = F_X(b) − F_X(a) giving P(X ∈ {a+1, …, b}). You instead want P(3 ≤ X ≤ 7) = P(X ∈ {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}). Which expression is correct?
options: F_X(7) − F_X(3), since both endpoints should be inclusive in the interval
F_X(7) − F_X(2), shifting the lower endpoint down by one to include the value 3
F_X(8) − F_X(3), shifting the upper endpoint up by one to include the value 7
F_X(7) + F_X(3), adding because both endpoints contribute mass to the interval
questions.hint: The formula excludes the lower endpoint. To include 3, pick a lower bound that excludes 2 (so 3 stays in).
questions.explanation: P(3 ≤ X ≤ 7) = P(2 < X ≤ 7) for integer X, so this equals F_X(7) − F_X(2). The rule: to include a value at the lower endpoint, shift it down by one (for integer X). This open-vs-closed-endpoint bookkeeping is one of the most common sources of off-by-one errors with CDFs.

distractorRationale.0: Direct application of the formula without adjusting for the lower-endpoint exclusion; off-by-one — drops X = 3
distractorRationale.2: Shifts the wrong endpoint; the upper end is already included in the formula, no adjustment needed there
distractorRationale.3: Forgot that interval probabilities are differences of CDF values, not sums — produces a value possibly exceeding 1

questions.question: For a discrete random variable, the CDF is flat (no jump) at some value x. What does this tell you about P(X = x)?
options: P(X = x) equals the height of the CDF curve at the point x where the flat region occurs
P(X = x) = 0, because jumps in the CDF are what encode probability mass
P(X = x) is undefined when the CDF has no jump there
P(X = x) = 1 − F_X(x), the complement of the CDF height
questions.hint: Jumps in the CDF encode probability mass. What does the absence of a jump mean?
questions.explanation: A flat region means no new probability mass accumulates there, so P(X = x) = 0 for all x in that region. The CDF still has a value (the running cumulative), but the random variable doesn't 'land on' those points. Where the CDF jumps by p, P(X = that point) = p.
questions.concept: Recovering PMF from CDF: jumps = probabilities

distractorRationale.0: Conflates the CDF value F_X(x) with the PMF value P(X = x); a common foundational confusion
distractorRationale.2: Treats the absence-of-jump as a definitional gap rather than as zero probability; the CDF is still well-defined and equals zero-step at flat points
distractorRationale.3: Confuses CDF complement with PMF; survival 1 − F_X(x) is not the same as point mass P(X = x)
